person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the land, water and energy required to grow lettuce hydroponically against conventionally, in Yuma, Arizona
span.quote: The land, water, and energy requirements of hydroponics were compared to those of conventional agriculture by example of lettuce production in Yuma, Arizona, USA.

span.label: whether hydroponic lettuce production is a more sustainable alternative to conventional production on land, water and energy together
span.quote: The land, water, and energy requirements of hydroponics were compared to those of conventional agriculture by example of lettuce production in Yuma, Arizona, USA.

span.label: the first quantitative land-water-energy comparison of conventional and hydroponic lettuce in the southwestern United States, identifying energy availability as the deciding factor
span.quote: To the authors’ knowledge, this is the first quantitative comparison of conventional and hydroponic produce production by example of lettuce grown in the southwestern United States.

span.label: existence
span.quote: Hydroponics offered 11 ± 1.7 times higher yields but required 82 ± 11 times more energy compared to conventionally produced lettuce.

span.label: agriculture already using 38.6% of ice-free land and 70% of withdrawn freshwater, against a growing population
span.quote: However, approximately 38.6% of the ice-free land and 70% of withdrawn freshwater is already devoted to agriculture

span.label: conventional figures taken from crop budgets and government agricultural statistics; hydroponic figures derived theoretically from engineering equations populated with literature values
span.term: conventional figures taken from crop budgets and government agricultural statistics; hydroponic figures derived theoretically from engineering equations populated with literature values
span.quote: Data were obtained from crop budgets and governmental agricultural statistics, and contrasted with theoretical data for hydroponic lettuce production derived by using engineering equations populated with literature values.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE TRADE IS LAND AND WATER AGAINST ENERGY, AND IT IS NOT A CLOSE CALL IN EITHER DIRECTION: 11x the yield per area and a fraction of the water, against 82x the energy per kilogram. Neither system dominates and the choice is set by which resource is scarce locally
span.quote: Hydroponics offered 11 ± 1.7 times higher yields but required 82 ± 11 times more energy compared to conventionally produced lettuce.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: SO THE ANSWER IS GEOGRAPHIC RATHER THAN TECHNOLOGICAL: the paper's remedy is to site the greenhouse where renewable energy is cheap, which converts a sustainability question into a siting question
span.quote: One possible way to make commercial hydroponics a more sustainable and suitable alternative would be to relocate the greenhouse to an area where there are cheap and renewable sources of energy, such as solar, geothermal or wind power

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: AND THE SOLAR OFFSET IS COMPUTED RATHER THAN ASSERTED: at 14% conversion and 6.5 kWh/m2, the greenhouse-to-panel area ratio needed to cover the full energy demand is about 1:3.0 - so the land saved by hydroponics is partly spent again on generating its energy
span.quote: Assuming a conversion efficiency of 14% and an average daily solar radiation value of 6.5 kWh per square meter per year \ [29\] the ratio of greenhouse to solar panel area that would be required to offset the full energy demand of the hydroponic system is approximately 1:3.0

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: AND EVEN THEN IT CANNOT RUN OFF-GRID: a 24-hour production cycle against seasonal and day-to-day variation in solar radiation requires a grid connection, so the 1:3.0 ratio is an energy balance and not an autonomy claim
span.quote: with an understanding that the 24-h production cycle along with seasonal and day-to-day changes in solar radiation would require the system to be connected to the electrical grid.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: SIMPLIFIED HYDROPONICS TRADES YIELD FOR ENERGY: abandoning the energy-intensive control equipment costs total yield and still out-performs conventional systems three- to four-fold on an area basis - which is the paper's own counterexample to its headline energy figure
span.quote: These operational changes come at the cost of total yield; however, such systems can still out-perform conventional systems by a factor of three to four on an area basis

span.label: conventional calculations assume one lettuce crop per year, while that land carries warm-season crops the rest of the year whose water and energy needs may differ
span.quote: To begin, the calculations for the conventional production of lettuce assumed that only one crop of lettuce can be grown in a given year. While this might be true, much of the land used to produce lettuce is dedicated to warm season crops when lettuce is not in production. It’s possible that these crops have water and energy requirements that differ from lettuce.

span.label: the hydroponic greenhouse was assumed to be commercial scale and optimised for maximum production - a best case
span.quote: Additionally, the hydroponic greenhouse was assumed to be of commercial scale and was optimized for maximum production.

span.label: one fixed greenhouse size at one site (Yuma), while real greenhouses vary in configuration and location; the authors say modelling several would be reasonable and could produce alternative results
span.quote: As such, it would be reasonable to model multiple hypothetical greenhouses. Changing the assumptions surrounding the hypothetical greenhouses could produce alternative results.

span.label: only DIRECT energy inputs were counted - energy embodied in chemical or material inputs was excluded
span.quote: In addition, this study solely focused on direct energy inputs to hydroponic and conventional lettuce production and did not consider energy embodied in chemical or material inputs.

span.label: no full life cycle assessment was performed, and the authors say one could produce alternative results with labour hours figuring prominently
span.quote: Performing a full life cycle assessment of hydroponics vs. conventional lettuce production could also produce alternative results, with labor hours potentially figuring prominently into the economic equation.

span.label: factors that could block implementation - energy scarcity and higher upfront capital costs - were not discussed
span.quote: Lastly, this study did not discuss additional factors that might inhibit the successful implementation of hydroponics, such as energy scarcity and higher upfront capital costs.

span.label: whether reduced food transport distance is a real benefit is left open, pending a life cycle assessment that considers transportation
span.quote: Performing a life cycle assessment that considers the environmental impact of food transportation could show whether this benefit of hydroponics is significant.

span.label: conventional figures were taken from crop budgets and government agricultural statistics rather than estimated, so one side of the comparison rests on observed production data
span.note: eliminates: estimation error on the conventional side of the comparison - those figures come from crop budgets and government statistics rather than from the authors' model. It does NOT eliminate it on the hydroponic side, which is theoretical throughout · outcome: held
span.quote: Data were obtained from crop budgets and governmental agricultural statistics, and contrasted with theoretical data for hydroponic lettuce production derived by using engineering equations populated with literature values.

span.label: all four headline quantities are reported with a standard deviation - yield, water and energy for both systems - so the 11x and 82x ratios carry their own uncertainty
span.note: eliminates: the 11x and 82x ratios being read as exact - every one of the four headline quantities carries a standard deviation · outcome: held
span.quote: Yields of lettuce per greenhouse unit (815 m2) of 41 ± 6.1 kg/m2/y had water and energy demands of 20 ± 3.8 L/kg/y and 90,000 ± 11,000 kJ/kg/y (±standard deviation), respectively.

span.label: the solar offset needed to cover the hydroponic energy demand was computed from stated conversion efficiency and radiation values rather than asserted, and the grid dependence is stated with it
span.note: eliminates: solar generation being asserted as a remedy without a cost - the greenhouse-to-panel area ratio is computed at about 1:3.0, and the grid dependence is stated with it, so the land saved is partly spent again · outcome: partial
span.quote: Assuming a conversion efficiency of 14% and an average daily solar radiation value of 6.5 kWh per square meter per year \ [29\] the ratio of greenhouse to solar panel area that would be required to offset the full energy demand of the hydroponic system is approximately 1:3.0

span.label: hydroponics
span.quote: The land, water, and energy requirements of hydroponics were compared to those of conventional agriculture by example of lettuce production in Yuma, Arizona, USA.

span.label: conventional agriculture
span.quote: Some of the negative impacts of conventional agriculture include the high and inefficient use of water, large land requirements, high concentrations of nutrients and pesticides in runoff, and soil degradation accompanied by erosion

span.label: simplified hydroponics
span.quote: An alternative scenario to consider is one in which much of the energy-intensive characteristics of advanced and commercial hydroponic operations are abandoned in favor of simpler systems, a practice known as “simplified hydroponics” or “popular hydroponics.”

span.label: life cycle assessment
span.quote: Performing a full life cycle assessment of hydroponics vs. conventional lettuce production could also produce alternative results, with labor hours potentially figuring prominently into the economic equation.

span.label: arable land
span.quote: This is still an improvement over conventional production, which uses ten times more land and water on a yield basis and requires arable land.

span.label: crop budgets
span.quote: Data were obtained from crop budgets and governmental agricultural statistics, and contrasted with theoretical data for hydroponic lettuce production derived by using engineering equations populated with literature values.

span.label: sustainability
span.quote: It identified energy availability as a major factor in assessing the sustainability of hydroponics, and it points to water-scarce settings offering an abundance of renewable energy (e.g., from solar, geothermal, or wind power) as particularly attractive regions for hydroponic agriculture.

span.label: greenhouse
span.quote: One possible way to make commercial hydroponics a more sustainable and suitable alternative would be to relocate the greenhouse to an area where there are cheap and renewable sources of energy, such as solar, geothermal or wind power

span.label: the `comparison` - ONE SIDE IS MEASURED AND THE OTHER IS MODELLED, and the abstract says so in a clause easy to read past: conventional figures come from CROP BUDGETS AND GOVERNMENT STATISTICS, hydroponic figures are THEORETICAL DATA DERIVED BY ENGINEERING EQUATIONS POPULATED WITH LITERATURE VALUES. So `11x higher yields, 82x more energy` compares an observed system with a calculated one. Legitimate, and not what a reader assumes from the word `comparison` - every quantity on this record inherits it
span.quote: Data were obtained from crop budgets and governmental agricultural statistics, and contrasted with theoretical data for hydroponic lettuce production derived by using engineering equations populated with literature values.

span.label: the hydroponic greenhouse - A SINGLE OPTIMISED HYPOTHETICAL, not a survey of installations: commercial scale, optimised for maximum production, one fixed size, sited in Yuma. The authors say hydroponic greenhouses `come in a variety of configurations and can be located almost anywhere` and that modelling several would be reasonable. The figures are therefore a best case at one site
span.quote: Furthermore, as seen in Equation (2), the greenhouse was assumed to be of a specific size and located in Yuma, Arizona (one of the most productive areas for lettuce grown conventionally in the United States). In reality, hydroponic greenhouses come in a variety of configurations and can be located almost anywhere.

span.label: `energy` here is DIRECT ENERGY ONLY - the study excludes energy embodied in chemical or material inputs, and excludes labour. The 82x ratio is a ratio of direct inputs, and the authors say a full life cycle assessment could produce alternative results
span.quote: In addition, this study solely focused on direct energy inputs to hydroponic and conventional lettuce production and did not consider energy embodied in chemical or material inputs.

span.label: `conventional agriculture` - DEFINED HISTORICALLY AND EXPLICITLY: growing crops in soil, in the open air, with irrigation and the active application of nutrients, pesticides and herbicides. A definition by PRACTICE rather than by yield or by certification, which is what makes the comparison well-posed
span.quote: “Conventional” or “modern industrial agriculture” has been historically defined as the practice of growing crops in soil, in the open air, with irrigation, and the active application of nutrients, pesticides, and herbicides.

span.label: critiques → the assumption that hydroponics is straightforwardly the more sustainable method - the authors conclude it cannot currently be deemed so for lettuce
span.quote: At this point in time, hydroponic farming of lettuce cannot be deemed a more sustainable alternative to conventional lettuce farming techniques, but it provides promising concepts that could lead to more sustainable food production.

span.label: hydroponics —contrasted-with→ conventional agriculture
span.quote: The land, water, and energy requirements of hydroponics were compared to those of conventional agriculture by example of lettuce production in Yuma, Arizona, USA.

span.label: simplified hydroponics —is-a→ hydroponics
span.quote: An alternative scenario to consider is one in which much of the energy-intensive characteristics of advanced and commercial hydroponic operations are abandoned in favor of simpler systems, a practice known as “simplified hydroponics” or “popular hydroponics.”

span.label: hydroponics —causes→ arable land
span.note: direction on the measure: eliminates · strength of the relation: 0.9
span.quote: Eliminating the need for arable land has other benefits including versatility in system siting and a potential reduction in the distance in which food must travel.

span.label: hydroponics gave 11 ± 1.7 times higher yields and required 82 ± 11 times more energy than conventional lettuce production
span.quote: Hydroponics offered 11 ± 1.7 times higher yields but required 82 ± 11 times more energy compared to conventionally produced lettuce.

span.label: hydroponic lettuce cannot currently be deemed a more sustainable alternative, though it uses land and water more efficiently
span.quote: At this point in time, hydroponic farming of lettuce cannot be deemed a more sustainable alternative to conventional lettuce farming techniques, but it provides promising concepts that could lead to more sustainable food production.

span.label: energy availability is the deciding factor, making water-scarce regions with abundant renewables the attractive sites
span.quote: It identified energy availability as a major factor in assessing the sustainability of hydroponics, and it points to water-scarce settings offering an abundance of renewable energy (e.g., from solar, geothermal, or wind power) as particularly attractive regions for hydroponic agriculture.

span.label: simplified hydroponics sacrifices yield but still out-performs conventional systems three- to four-fold on an area basis
span.quote: These operational changes come at the cost of total yield; however, such systems can still out-perform conventional systems by a factor of three to four on an area basis

span.label: conventional agriculture
span.quote: “Conventional” or “modern industrial agriculture” has been historically defined as the practice of growing crops in soil, in the open air, with irrigation, and the active application of nutrients, pesticides, and herbicides. Some of the negative impacts of conventional agriculture include the high and inefficient use of water, large land requirements

span.label: hydroponic: 41 ± 6.1 kg/m2/y yield, 20 ± 3.8 L/kg/y water, 90,000 ± 11,000 kJ/kg/y energy, per 815 m2 greenhouse unit — None
span.quote: Yields of lettuce per greenhouse unit (815 m2) of 41 ± 6.1 kg/m2/y had water and energy demands of 20 ± 3.8 L/kg/y and 90,000 ± 11,000 kJ/kg/y (±standard deviation), respectively.

span.quote: In comparison, conventional production yielded 3.9 ± 0.21 kg/m2/y of produce, with water and energy demands of 250 ± 25 L/kg/y and 1100 ± 75 kJ/kg/y, respectively.

span.quote: However, approximately 38.6% of the ice-free land and 70% of withdrawn freshwater is already devoted to agriculture
